title: Uranus is tipped on its side, so each pole gets 42 years of sunlight, then 42 of night

cover.alt: Uranus in infrared from the Webb telescope: a pale blue globe with a bright white polar cap, circled by thin glowing rings, with tiny moons around it.
cover.credit: NASA, ESA, CSA, STScI · CC BY 4.0

body: The spin axis of Uranus lies **almost flat in the plane of the Solar System**, so the planet rolls around the Sun on its side. Over its 84-year orbit, first one pole and then the other points towards the Sun. So each pole gets around 42 years of continuous sunlight followed by 42 years of darkness, while near the equinoxes the Sun shines on the equator and day and night alternate. Nobody knows for certain why it is tipped over; the usual speculation is that an Earth-sized protoplanet crashed into it while the Solar System was forming.

slides.question: By how many degrees is the axis of Uranus tilted?
slides.explanation: 97.77°, which leaves its spin axis nearly in the plane of its orbit around the Sun.

steps.label: One pole faces the Sun for years on end
Equinox: the Sun shines on the equator
Now the other pole faces the Sun
Equinox again, then back to the start

slides.label: 49 K: the lowest minimum temperature of any planet in the Solar System
slides.text: Uranus gives off far less internal heat than the other giant planets, and why is still not understood.

slides.heading: Strange, still
slides.text: You might expect the sunlit poles to be warmest, yet Uranus is hotter at its equator than at its poles, and nobody knows why. Only one spacecraft has ever visited: Voyager 2 flew past in January 1986.

slides.question: William Herschel found Uranus in 1781. What made it a first?
options: First planet found with a telescope
First planet found to have moons
slides.explanation: Herschel first observed it on 13 March 1781, making Uranus the first planet identified as such with the aid of a telescope.
